about: Jeremy's learn-anything goal, recorded live 2026-11-04 (qwen3.8:27b-mlx, one strip call and one composing call, clean first try, 5 min 48 s): links or documents, a brief, study cards, a toolkit, saved to a folder. Two source stages make links and the folder optional with one either-or group; study_cards after write_brief takes its material from the brief; the composing answer re-declared a dead `material` input, which the merge drops.

request.goal: Okay, for this task I would like to use it to learn a new thing.  I will give you a list of things like URLs or documents, and you will generate a summary, diagram, flash cards, cheat sheets or glossarie; also generate a prompt that can be used to have an interactive conversation with an AI, and also generate a succinctly written mass of succinct paragraphs which can be used to feed a voice transcription model to have it read things to me.
request.name: Learn stuff

stages.name: Read the Links
stages.why: Fetch each URL you give and pull out what every page says about your topic, with exact quotes (web scraping).

stages.name: Read the Documents
stages.why: Read every file in a folder you point to and pull out what each says about your topic, with quotes and page numbers (document parsing).

stages.name: Write the Summary
stages.why: Turn everything gathered from the links and documents into one brief that answers your topic and cites every point by file, page, or link.

stages.name: Make Study Cards
stages.why: Turn the brief into flashcards and a short quiz so you can test yourself on what you just read.

stages.name: Build the Toolkit
stages.why: From the brief and cards, produce a structural diagram of the topic, a cheat sheet or glossary of key terms, a conversation prompt for an interactive AI session, and a set of short, plain paragraphs written for a voice transcription model to read aloud to you.

stages.name: Deliver
stages.why: Write the summary, study cards, diagram, cheat sheet, conversation prompt, and voice script as files into a folder you choose.

recipe.name: Jeremy Learn Stuff
recipe.description: Give a focus, some links, and/or a folder of documents; get a summary, a concept map, a cheat sheet, study cards, a conversation prompt, and a voice script, all saved as files in a folder you choose.

focus.label: Focus
focus.description: The topic or question you want to learn about.

urls.label: Links to read
urls.description: One link per line. Each page is fetched and read for the focus.

folder.label: Documents folder
folder.description: A folder of PDFs, Word docs, Markdown, or text files to read.

material.label: Material for study cards
material.description: The text to turn into flashcards and a quiz. Paste the summary or any notes here.

output_folder.label: Output folder
output_folder.description: Where the summary, cards, diagram, cheat sheet, conversation prompt, and voice script are written as files.

reader.description: Reads pages and documents and pulls out findings about the focus.

writer.description: Writes the summary, cheat sheet, conversation prompt, voice script, and formats study cards.

mapper.description: Turns the brief into a structured concept map (a Knowledge Spine).

diagram.label: Concept Map
diagram.description: A visual map of the topic's key concepts and how they connect.

cheat_sheet.label: Cheat Sheet
cheat_sheet.description: A quick-reference glossary and key points from the topic.

conversation_prompt.label: Conversation Prompt
conversation_prompt.description: A prompt to paste into any AI chat for an interactive study session.

voice_script.label: Voice Script
voice_script.description: Short, plain paragraphs written to be read aloud by a voice model.

stages.name: Build the Toolkit
stages.why: The brief and cards become a concept map (a diagram of how ideas connect), a cheat sheet of key terms, a prompt for an interactive AI conversation, and short plain paragraphs ready to feed a voice reader.

stages.name: Deliver
stages.why: Everything the toolkit built is written as files into the folder you choose, so you can keep, share, or open them anywhere.

files.text:
You are a learning designer. You receive a **brief**: a summary of a topic with citations to its sources.

Produce a Knowledge Spine: a structured map of the topic's key concepts and how they connect.

## What to produce

A JSON object with exactly these fields:

- `title` (string): the name of the topic, taken from the brief.
- `concepts` (array): 6 to 15 concept objects, each with:
  - `id` (string): a short kebab-case identifier, e.g. `neural-network`, `backpropagation`.
  - `name` (string): a human-readable name for the concept.
  - `prerequisites` (array of strings): ids of concepts that must be understood before this one. May be empty.
  - `related` (array of strings): ids of concepts that are related but are not prerequisites. May be empty.

## Rules

- Extract concepts only from the brief. Do not invent concepts the brief does not mention.
- Every id that appears in `prerequisites` or `related` must match an `id` in the `concepts` array.
- Order the concepts roughly from foundational to advanced.
- Output only the JSON object. No preamble, no explanation, no markdown fences.

You are a study-aid writer. You receive a **brief**: a summary of a topic with citations to its sources.

Write a cheat sheet and glossary for the topic.

## What to produce

A Markdown document with these sections, in order:

1. **Key Terms** — a glossary of the most important terms from the brief. Each entry: the term in bold, then a one-sentence definition.
2. **Quick Reference** — the most important facts, formulas, or steps, in a compact bulleted list.
3. **Common Pitfalls** — mistakes or confusions a learner is likely to make, each with a brief correction.
4. **Further Reading** — any sources, topics, or links the brief mentions that go deeper.

## Rules

- Stay inside the brief. Do not add outside knowledge.
- Keep each entry to one or two sentences.
- When a point comes from a specific source in the brief, cite it (file name, page number, or link).
- No preamble. Start with the first heading.

You are a conversation designer. You receive a **brief**: a summary of a topic with citations to its sources.

Write a single prompt that a user can paste into any AI chat (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, etc.) to start an interactive study session on the topic.

## What to produce

One block of text — the prompt itself, ready to paste. It should:

- Open by naming the topic and its scope, drawn from the brief.
- Tell the AI to act as a patient tutor who explains, quizzes, and checks understanding.
- List the key concepts the AI should cover, taken from the brief.
- Ask the AI to start by asking the learner what they already know, then adapt the session.
- Note that the AI should cite the brief's sources when it can.

## Rules

- Output only the prompt text. No preamble, no explanation of what the prompt does, no markdown fences around it.
- Keep it under 400 words.
- Stay inside the brief for all topic content. Do not add outside knowledge.

You are a script writer for a voice reader. You receive a **brief**: a summary of a topic with citations to its sources.

Write a set of short, plain paragraphs that a text-to-speech model will read aloud to the listener.

## What to produce

A sequence of short paragraphs (3 to 6 sentences each), in plain spoken English. The script should:

- Open with one sentence that says what the topic is and why it matters.
- Walk through the main ideas in order, one paragraph per idea.
- Use simple words and short sentences. When a technical term is unavoidable, say it plainly and explain it in the next sentence.
- Close with one paragraph that ties the ideas together and suggests what to explore next.

## Rules

- Stay inside the brief. Do not add outside knowledge.
- No headings, no bullet points, no citations in the text (the listener cannot see them).
- No preamble. Start with the first paragraph.
- Aim for 400 to 800 words total.
- Output only the script text. No markdown fences.

You are a study-aid formatter. You receive **cards**: a JSON object with a `cards` array. Each card has `front` (the question or prompt), `back` (the answer), and `topic` (a short label).

## What to produce

A Markdown document that lays out the cards for study:

- Group cards by `topic` under a heading for each topic.
- For each card, show the front as a bold question, then the answer on the next line in a blockquote.
- End with a **Quiz** section that lists 3 to 5 questions drawn from the cards. Hide each answer inside a Markdown `<details>` block so the learner can reveal it.

## Rules

- Do not change the content of any card. Only reformat.
- No preamble. Start with the first topic heading.
- Output only the Markdown. No markdown fences around the whole document.
